newsitem.title: USA: No ag cuts under US budget pact-Congress staffers.
newsitem.headline: No ag cuts under US budget pact-Congress staffers.

text.p: U.S. farm programs would see no significant cuts, if any, under the proposal to balance the federal budget by 2002, congressional staff workers said Monday.
Andy Fisher, spokesman for the Senate Agriculture Committee, said preliminary indications were "no reconciliation (cuts) for agriculture."
A high-ranking House Agriculture Committee staff worker said detailed documents were not available yet but, "We know of no reconciliation instructions that affect agriculture at all."
The pact was announced at the end of last week by the White House and leaders of the Republican-controlled Congress.

Analyst Bill Lesher said he believed agriculture "won't have a cut that's significant at all, if any." He said the House was more likely than the Senate to seek cuts in the ag budget but any proposed cuts would not stick.

Still to be seen, Lesher said, was how a freeze on discretionary spending might affect agriculture-related programs and whether an attack on "corporate welfare" would touch programs like Export Enhancement Program, Market Access Program, ethanol tax breaks and Rural Electrification Administration lending programs.
Last year's passage of the "Freedom to Farm" law, with its fixed annual payments to farmers, helped assure the farm program would not be subject to cuts, Fisher said.

A potential sticking point under the discretionary freeze would be the administration proposal for $390 million in meat inspection fees. If the idea is rejected, as meatpackers hope, an offsetting cut would be needed elsewhere.
